hashing_fundamentals.name: Hashing and Hash Functions
hashing_fundamentals.definition: Hashing is a technique that maps large keys of variable sizes into fixed-size values (hash codes) using a mathematical Hash Function, allowing constant-time O(1) average search, insertion, and deletion in a Hash Table.
hashing_fundamentals.hash_table_concept: A Hash Table is an associative array where keys are converted by a hash function h(key) into an array index where the corresponding value or record is stored.
hash_function_properties: Uniform Distribution: Distributes keys evenly across all table slots to minimize collisions.
Deterministic: The same key must always produce the exact same hash index.
Computational Efficiency: Fast to compute in O(1) time.
Common Hash Functions: Division method (h(k) = k % m where m is prime), Multiplication method, Mid-square method, Folding method.
hashing_fundamentals.load_factor: The load factor alpha = n / m (where n = number of stored elements, m = total table size). When alpha exceeds 0.70 - 0.75, rehashing into a larger table (often double size) is performed to prevent performance degradation.

viva_questions.q: What is a collision in a hash table?
viva_questions.a: A collision occurs when two distinct keys k1 != k2 produce the exact same hash index: h(k1) == h(k2).

viva_questions.q: Why is the table size m typically chosen as a prime number in division hashing?
viva_questions.a: Choosing a prime number reduces the likelihood of common factors with keys, thereby producing a more uniform distribution and drastically reducing collisions.

collision_resolution.name: Collision Resolution Techniques
collision_resolution.definition: Collision resolution techniques handle the situation where multiple keys map to the same hash table index. The two primary categories are Separate Chaining (Open Hashing) and Open Addressing (Closed Hashing).

techniques.separate_chaining: Each hash table slot points to a linked list of records that share the same hash code. Inserting is O(1), search is O(1 + alpha). Never overflows.
techniques.open_addressing: All elements are stored directly inside the hash table array. If a collision occurs, alternative slots are probed:
techniques.linear_probing: Sequentially searches the next slot: h(k, i) = (h'(k) + i) % m. Suffers from Primary Clustering (long contiguous blocks of occupied cells).
techniques.quadratic_probing: Probes with quadratic intervals: h(k, i) = (h'(k) + c1*i + c2*i^2) % m. Avoids primary clustering but can suffer from Secondary Clustering.
techniques.double_hashing: Uses a second independent hash function: h(k, i) = (h1(k) + i * h2(k)) % m. Excellent distribution, virtually eliminates clustering.

collision_resolution.comparison_table:
| Parameter | Separate Chaining (Open Hashing) | Open Addressing (Closed Hashing) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Storage Mechanism** | External linked lists per slot | Everything stored inside the array |
| **Capacity Limit** | Can store more elements than table size (alpha > 1) | Cannot exceed table size (alpha <= 1) |
| **Deletions** | Simple linked list node deletion | Requires dummy DELETED markers to prevent broken probe chains |
| **Memory Overhead** | Pointer overhead per node | Extra space reserved in advance |
| **Clustering** | No clustering | Primary (linear) or Secondary (quadratic) clustering |

collision_resolution.dry_run:
Insert Keys: 10, 17, 24 with Table Size = 7
1. Key 10: h(10) = 10 % 7 = 3. Slot 3 is EMPTY. Store 10 at [3].
2. Key 17: h(17) = 17 % 7 = 3. Slot 3 has 10 (COLLISION!).
   Probe i=1: (3 + 1) % 7 = 4. Slot 4 is EMPTY. Store 17 at [4].
3. Key 24: h(24) = 24 % 7 = 3. Slot 3 occupied (10), Slot 4 occupied (17).
   Probe i=2: (3 + 2) % 7 = 5. Slot 5 is EMPTY. Store 24 at [5].
Search Key 17: h(17) = 3. arr[3]=10 != 17. Next: arr[4]=17 == 17! Found in 2 probes.
collision_resolution.time_complexity:
• Best Case: O(1)
• Average Case: O(1) (Under low load factor alpha < 0.7)
• Worst Case: O(n) (When all keys collide into the same slot/chain)
collision_resolution.space_complexity: O(m) where m is table size.
collision_resolution.applications: Compiler symbol tables, database indexing, caching (Redis/Memcached), cryptographic verification, associative arrays in languages like Python dict and JavaScript Map.

viva_questions.q: What is primary clustering in linear probing?
viva_questions.a: Primary clustering occurs when occupied slots cluster together in contiguous blocks. Any key hashing into or near this block increases its length, exponentially increasing search and insertion times.

viva_questions.q: How does Double Hashing prevent clustering?
viva_questions.a: Double hashing uses a second hash function h2(k) as the probe step size: probe = (h1(k) + i * h2(k)) % m. Different keys that collide under h1(k) take different probe jump sizes, breaking up clusters.
